    Sprint 3 – Moving From Basic To Agentic RAG

    📄

    Agent integrations with RAG systems

    Lesson 1

    Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems combine large language models with external knowledge bases to produce accurate, context-informed responses. Traditional RAG pipelines are static - given a query, they retrieve relevant documents and feed them to an LLM for a one-shot answer. Agent-integrated RAG (often called agentic RAG) takes this a step further by embedding an AI agent into the pipeline to dynamically decide how and when to use retrieval or other tools. Last week we already built a simple version of a system that would be considered Agentic RAG, this week we dive a bit deeper to explore the entire potential pipeline and Agentic system design patterns in general. This article will discuss why agentic RAG is useful, practical architecture patterns, agent decision logic, and how agent actions interface with retrievers.



    Recap: Traditional RAG Pipeline and Its Limitations


    Traditional RAG Pipeline: In a basic RAG system, an embedding model converts the user query to a vector and retrieves similar documents from a vector database (the knowledge base). The retrieved context is then combined with the query and passed to an LLM to generate the. Advanced RAG implementations may include hybrid search (combining vector similarity with keyword search), re-ranking of retrieved data, prompt templates for better grounding and prompt or tool registries to manage multiple resources.


    Limitations of Static RAG: While powerful, static RAG has several well-known limitations. First, it is limited to the data in the vector database - it cannot easily fetch real-time data or external information beyond its indexed knowledge. If the user asks about a very recent event or something outside the indexed domain, a static RAG system simply has no mechanism to find relevant info. Second, a static pipeline performs a single retrieval pass for a query. If the retrieval step fails (e.g. returns irrelevant documents due to a poorly formed query or embedding miss), the LLM will either not know the answer or worse, hallucinate using unrelated context. The static system will not reflect on itself and fix the issue because it has no feedback loop - it doesn’t know if the retrieved data is actually relevant or sufficient. Finally, static RAG lacks adaptability. It treats each query independently and follows a fixed sequence - it cannot plan multi-step strategies for answering complex queries. These limitations are exactly what motivates introducing an agent into the loop to add reasoning and decision-making.



    Agentic RAG: Adaptive Retrieval with AI Agents


    In short, Agentic RAG is a system that uses AI agents to enhance RAG’s flexibility and accuracy. An agent in this context is an LLM enabled with decision-making abilities and tool-use capabilities via smart prompt engineering. Instead of always blindly retrieving and answering, an agentic system allows the LLM to decide if, when, and how to retrieve information - or even to use other tools that are not retrieval bound in general sense - based on the query and intermediate results. The agent effectively controls the RAG workflow. In practice, this means the LLM can perform multi-step reasoning - analyze the query, decide to fetch information from one or multiple sources, possibly verify or refine that information, and only then compose a final answer. This is different from static, single-pass querying and becomes an adaptive, iterative approach. 


    Key Agent Capabilities - Agentic systems leverage capabilities that go beyond a basic RAG loop (most of them we covered last week):


    • Tool Use: The agent (LLM) can invoke external functions (tools) such as search engines, database queries, calculators, or other APIs. In our case, the primary tools are retrievers that fetch relevant context. By calling tools, the agent can incorporate new information on the fly. Also, it is able to call multiple searches in a single turn.

    • Step-by-Step Reasoning: Instead of responding immediately, the agent can break complex tasks into sub-steps or iterative queries. This includes query planning (decomposing a complex question into simpler ones) and conditional decision-making based on intermediate results. For example, an agent confronted with a broad question might first ask itself: “Do I need to lookup multiple pieces of information? Which should I find first?” and plan out those retrievals.

    • Memory and State: Agents maintain state across turns, allowing them to remember what was retrieved or decided in previous steps. This short-term memory (often maintained as a message history or state object) lets the agent build on prior tool outputs. Over longer interactions, agents can also have long-term memory (caches or conversation history) to stay consistent.

    • Autonomy and Adaptability: With the above abilities, the agent can adapt to changing requirements. For example, if one knowledge source fails to produce an answer, it can try another source or a different approach. Compared to a static pipeline that requires human tuning of prompts for every edge case, an agent can self-correct and iterate until it finds a solution (within reasonable limits of course).


    Benefits Over Traditional RAG: Agentic RAG brings several clear improvements. It offers flexibility to pull data from multiple knowledge bases or APIs in one session, whereas a standard RAG pipeline typically queries a single vector store. It is more adaptive, moving from a rigid retrieve-then-answer sequence to a more intelligent workflow that can come up with workflow strategies in real time. Accuracy can improve because the agent can validate and refine its results - the system no longer blindly trusts the first retrieval results if they seem off. It can also scale to multi-modal data and multi-agent collaboration.


    Trade-offs: It’s important to note that agentic RAG isn’t a silver bullet for all cases. This increased intelligence comes at the cost of greater complexity. Multi-step agent reasoning means more LLM calls (higher latency and API costs) and more moving parts that need robust handling and evaluation. Agents are also not perfect - they still get confused, hallucinate tool usages, or enter loops if not properly constrained. In practice, engineers must carefully design the agent’s logic and put guardrails in place. With that context, let’s dive into how we can implement these agents using LangGraph.



    Architecture Patterns for Agentic RAG


    There is no single “right” design for an agent-augmented RAG system; the architecture depends on the use case. However, several common patterns have emerged. Few of them being: (1) Retrieval Agent for selective context use, (2) Corrective RAG with query refinement, and (3) Multi-tool retrieval agents.



    Retrieval Agent: Deciding When to Retrieve


    One of the simplest agent integrations is to allow the LLM to decide whether it actually needs external knowledge to answer a query. In a static RAG pipeline, we always retrieve documents for every query, but sometimes this is unnecessary (for example, the user might just say “Hello” or ask a trivial question). An agent can conditionally skip retrieval and respond directly when appropriate.This saves time and compute, and reduces opportunities for confusion by not retrieving irrelevant data for simple queries.

    How it works: We configure the LLM with a retriever tool and prompt it to use the tool only if needed. For example, using LangGraph, we might have a node called generate_query_or_respond that takes the conversation state (which includes the latest user message) and calls an LLM. This LLM is bound to a tool like retrieve_context, which is essentially a function that searches the vector database. The agent’s prompt or few-shot examples should encourage a behavior like: “If the user asks a factual question that might need external info, use the search tool to fetch relevant info. If the user prompt can be answered directly from your knowledge or is a casual conversation, respond directly without using a tool”. 


    In practice, when this node is executed, the LLM will output either (a) a direct answer (with no tool usage), or (b) a special action indicating a tool should be invoked. If you are using LangGraph for example, the graph workflow workflow can then branch based on this output. Specifically, we add a conditional edge that checks: did the model call the retriever tool? If yes, transition to a Retrieve or a more general Tool node, if no (meaning the model produced a final answer), we end the process. This conditional routing can be implemented by a small function that inspects the model’s last message for tool usage.


    Interfacing with the Retriever: The retriever itself is just like the one in a normal RAG system, but here it’s packaged as a tool that the agent can invoke. When the agent gives a signal to call it, LangGraph’s tool-handling node will execute the retrieval and return the results as a message in the agent’s state (tagged as a ToolMessage in LangChain’s universe). At the next step, the agent gets to see the content of the retrieved documents in the conversation context. Essentially, the agent’s state might now contain: User’s question -> Assistant’s action calling the tool -> Tool’s answer (retrieved text). Having this information, the agent can continue reasoning. If we had gone down the “no retrieval needed” path, the agent would have just produced an answer and ended the flow. This retrieval agent pattern brings a small but important improvement: the agent’s reasoning can decide to avoid unnecessary retrieval or handle simple queries gracefully, making the system more efficient and user-friendly.



    Corrective RAG: Multi-Step Retrieval with Query Refinement


    A more advanced pattern that addresses one of the issues noted in the previous one - what if the initial retrieval fails or is insufficient? In a static pipeline, the user might just get a wrong or unhelpful answer. An agentic approach can detect this situation and correct it by iterating. In the industry this pattern is called Corrective RAG, as it aligns with the Corrective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (CRAG) strategy. At a high level, the agent will verify the quality of retrieved documents and decide either to proceed to answer or to refine the query and try again (possibly using a different tool like a web search).


    Workflow: When a new question comes in, the agent first retrieves documents from the vector DB (just like traditional RAG). Next, instead of immediately using them to answer, the agent runs a grading step: an LLM-based function that examines the retrieved text and judges if it’s relevant to the question. This can be implemented as a node (say grade_documents) that takes the question and the retrieved context, and outputs a simple verdict (relevant or not). For example, a prompt to this grader LLM might be: “Here is the user’s question and a retrieved document. Does the document contain information that helps answer the question? Answer yes or no”. If the documents are classified as adequate, our agent moves forward to the answer generation step. If documents are irrelevant (or if nothing was retrieved at all), the agent triggers a query refinement process. This typically involves two sub-steps: (a) use the LLM to rewrite the user’s question into a better query (perhaps more specific or using alternate keywords), and (b) use a different retriever tool (like a web search API or a second vector store) with the revised query to fetch additional information. Finally, the agent combines whatever relevant info it has (from the vector DB and/or the web) and generates a final answer.


    In LangGraph, this entire loop can be constructed as a directed graph of nodes with conditional edges (which is much cleaner than handling all this logic in one giant prompt). In the figure above, we see one implementation of this pattern. The agent begins by potentially using a tool and then the flow splits - a grading node leads either to the answer node or to a rewrite node, which in turn goes back to retry retrieval. The condition logic on the edge after grading will look at the grader’s output: if the grader returned “yes, relevant”, go to the answer node, if “no”, go to the query rewrite node. The rewrite node produces a new user query (essentially replacing or refining the original question in the state), and then we loop back to the retrieval step (or we might even use an alternate tool here, such as a web_search_tool). This loop can iterate multiple times, though in practice you’d set it to only loop once or a limited number of times for efficiency.


    Why it helps: This corrective pattern significantly improves robustness. The agent actively verifies its knowledge before answering, reducing the chance of using irrelevant data or hallucinating. If the agent’s own knowledge base doesn’t cover the answer, it can fetch real-time or external data to fill the gap. For example, imagine asking an enterprise chatbot about “this quarter’s revenue” when the vector store only has data up to last year. A static RAG might give an outdated answer. An agentic RAG could realize no relevant document was retrieved, reformulate the query, and use a web search or database query to get the latest info, then answer accurately. This approach essentially augments static knowledge with live data and iterative checking, addressing two major static RAG limitations (stale data and irrelevant context) in one design.


    From an engineering perspective, implementing this with LangGraph means writing small, testable functions for each piece (retrieval, grading, rewriting, answering) and letting the framework handle the decision routing. It encourages a modular design - for instance, you could swap out the web search tool or adjust the grading criteria without rewriting the entire agent logic. A key best practice here is to craft solid prompts for grading and rewriting - these are specialized prompts distinct from the final answer prompt. Using structured outputs (e.g., utilising Pydantic models with boolean outputs) can make it easier to parse and route decisions reliably.



    Multi-Tool and Multi-Source Agents


    In more complex applications, an agent may have multiple retrievers and tools available to it - not just one vector database. For example, suppose we’re building a shopping assistant. It might have a vector index of inventory, another index of reviews, and access to a web search API. A static pipeline would struggle to combine these sources or choose the right one for a given question. An agent, however, can intelligently route queries and aggregate information from several sources.


    Routing to the Right Knowledge Source: One approach is to use a routing agent (sometimes called a router) that examines the query and decides which tool or knowledge base is most likely to have the answer. This could be implemented as a classification step (perhaps a simple if/else or another LLM prompt that outputs a tool name). For instance, if the query mentions “earphones”, use the regular Available Items retriever retriever, if it mentions “good reviews about lasting time”, use the Reviews retriever and potentially retrieve item IDs together with the context chunks, if it’s something general or not found in those, use web search to look for options in partner stores. In LangGraph, you might encode this logic either within the LLM agent’s prompt (i.e. let the LLM choose the tool based on descriptions) or as a separate preprocessing step. This kind of flexibility is exactly what the benefit is: an agentic RAG app can pull data from multiple sources and even use tools beyond just retrieval, whereas a standard RAG is usually tethered to one dataset.


    Multi-step Use of Multiple Tools: An even more dynamic scenario is when the agent might use several tools in sequence to answer a single query. For example, consider a user asks: “Could you suggest a laptop from available ones? Also, can you make sure that there is enough evidence from the previous buyers that the suggested items will last long?” An agent might take the following steps: (1) use a vector DB tool to find the laptops that would fit general requirements, (2) another vector DB tool that would prefilter the index on only the items retrieved in the first pass and then perform a search on user reviews, (3) respond with the items that match the initial query (I.e. laptops that have positive reviews about durability). In LangGraph, you can allow such flows by having the agent loop back into itself after a tool use (very similar to the ReAct pattern of reasoning). Essentially, the agent can alternate between reasoning (LLM node) and taking actions (Tool node) multiple times. The state carries over, so the agent’s next action can depend on all previously gathered info.


    One concrete implementation of a multi-tool loop is to have a graph with just two main nodes: an Agent node (LLM that can output tool calls or a final answer) and a Tool executor node. The Agent node outputs either a final answer or one or more tool calls - a conditional edge sends the flow to the Tool node if there is a tool call, otherwise to the End. The Tool node runs the requested tool(s) (retrieving docs, or doing whatever action) and returns the results, which get appended to the state as new messages. Then the graph loops back to the Agent node, so the agent now sees the tool results and can decide the next step. This is effectively an implementation of the ReAct agent framework within a RAG system - the agent Reasons, Acts (with tools), and then Observes the results in a loop until it can finally answer.



    A fully fleshed out Agentic RAG System


    In general, there is no single blueprint of what shape the Agentic RAG system should take in your specific use case. It is always the game of trade offs - adding more agency to the system increases it's complexity and latency but improves it's precision and accuracy. Consequentially, it is worth trying to conceptualise a fully fleshed out Agentic RAG system, this is how it could look like:


    1. Analysis of the user query: we pass the original user query to a LLM based Agent for analysis. This is where:

      • The original query can be rewritten, sometimes multiple times to create either a single or multiple queries to be passed down the pipeline.

      • The agent decides if additional data sources are required to answer the query.

    2. If additional data is required, the Retrieval step is triggered. In Agentic RAG, we could have a single or multiple agents responsible for figuring out what data sources should be tapped into, few examples:

      • Real time user data. This is a powerful concept as we might have some real time information like the current location of the user.

      • Internal documents that a user might be interested in.

      • Data available on the web via a web search tool.

      • …

    3. Retrieved data is consolidated and Reranked by a more powerful model compared to regular embedder. Data points are significantly narrowed down.

    4. If there is no need for additional data, we try to compose the final answer (or multiple answers or a set of actions) by prompting an LLM.

    5. The answer gets analysed, summarised and evaluated for correctness and relevance:

      • If the Agent decides that the answer is good enough, it gets returned to the user.

      • If the Agent decides that the answer needs improvement, we try to rewrite the user query and repeat the generation loop (this number of times the loop could run should be capped at a certain number).


    Having the above in mind, try simplifying wherever possible - only add additional steps if the validation of your system shows inadequate results.



    Agent Decision Logic and Best Practices


    Designing an agent integration involves careful thought about decision logic at each step - I.e., how does the agent know what to do next? Some of this is handled implicitly by the LLM (guided by prompts), and some can be enforced explicitly via code or conditions in the graph. Here are some best practices for multi-step decision-making with RAG agents:


    • Clear Prompt Instructions: The agent’s system prompt and examples should define the policy. For example, if using the retrieval-or-answer agent, make it explicit: “If the user’s question can be answered from the provided context, answer directly. If not, use the retrieve_context tool to find relevant information”. By anchoring the LLM with such rules, you reduce random behavior. Similarly, for multiple tools, provide a description of when to use each tool. Think of this as programming the agent through prompt engineering - it’s critical even for most powerful LLMs. As we now know from last week’s materials, most of the prompt engineering for tool usage is implemented by constructing accurate and descriptive docstrings for the functions to be used as tools or potentially exposed via MCP Servers which we are going to dig deeper into this week. 

    • Chain-of-Thought and Justification: Encourage the agent to internally reason before acting. In ReAct-style prompting, the model might produce a “Thought” explaining why it’s doing something, followed by an “Action”. With function-calling models, this thought process might be hidden, but you can simulate it via few-shot examples. The aim is to have the agent only call the retriever when it truly doesn’t know the answer or needs evidence. A useful practice is to include a couple of example QA pairs in the prompt: one where no tool is needed and one where the tool is needed, to model the decision process. This helps the LLM learn in context about when to stop vs when to search.

    • Limit the Loop & Use Safeguards: Multi-step agents can, in theory, loop forever (imagine an agent that keeps searching because it’s not satisfied). To prevent this, set a maximum number of iterations. E.g. LangGraph doesn’t loop indefinitely unless you tell it, but if your graph has a cycle (Like the ReAct type of agent we built last week), you should incorporate a counter or a stopping condition. For instance, after rewriting the query once, maybe stop and answer with whatever you have. Another safeguard is to detect repetition - if the agent is asking the same query again and again, break out. Additionally, always have a default end condition. Make sure that the path to the end condition always exists and is taken under reasonable conditions (even if the answer might be “I’m sorry, I cannot find the information”).

    • Validation and Moderation: Just as we used an LLM to grade document relevance, you can use similar techniques to validate the final answer (fact-checking against sources, or checking it meets some criteria). In production systems, it’s a good practice to include a step (or a parallel process) that evaluates the agent’s output for safety and correctness. It could also be a human approval step if needed. For example, an agent might draft an answer and then a separate verifier node could flag if the answer seems to contradict known data or lacks citation, etc., prompting the agent to reconsider.

    • Observability and Debugging: Multi-step reasoning can be hard to follow, so you must instrument your agent. Logging each agent thought and action is invaluable for debugging issues in the logic. If the agent made a poor decision, the trace can show you the prompt and state it had at that moment, so you can refine the prompt or logic.

    • Real-World Constraints: Keep the user experience and system constraints in mind. If using many tools or complex reasoning, the response will be slower – not every user query accepts that. One approach is to reserve the full agentic workflow for queries that are complex or high-stakes, and let simple queries use a simpler path. You could implement a lightweight classifier at the very start (e.g. detect if this looks like a straightforward factual question or a conversational prompt) and bypass the agent if not needed. This hybrid strategy ensures you are not always paying the cost of multi-step reasoning when a single-step RAG would do.


    Testing with Real Data: Finally, test the integrated system with actual use-case questions. Agents can behave unpredictably on edge cases. By testing, you might discover, for example, that your agent tends to always use the web search even when the answer was in the vector DB (maybe due to prompt wording bias). These insights will help you tweak the prompts or tool descriptions (maybe emphasize the internal data source first, and web as fallback). A/B testing agentic vs static RAG on your specific metrics (like answer accuracy, user satisfaction) will quantify the benefit and help justify the added complexity.



    How Agentic Reasoning Enhances RAG


    Stepping back, it’s worth summarizing how agent integrations improve or sometimes replace static retrieval in practice:


    • Selective and Contextual Retrieval: An agent can choose when to retrieve and what to retrieve based on context. Static RAG always does the same thing (e.g. top-5 similarity matches). The agent might decide to do a keyword search for a rare term instead of a semantic search, or skip retrieval if the answer is obvious. This contextual decision-making often yields more relevant info and avoids overwhelming the LLM with unnecessary text.

    • Iterative Deepening of Search: With an agent, the retrieval process can become iterative - initial retrieval yields some clues, which lead the agent to ask a more focused follow-up question, retrieving more specific info, and so on. This is similar to how a human researcher might conduct research - gradually narrowing in on the answer. It enables answering more complex queries that require multiple pieces of information or reasoning steps to synthesize an answer (something a single-pass RAG would most likely fail at).

    • Tool Synergy: Agents can incorporate tools beyond document retrieval. For example, if a question requires a calculation with retrieved data (perhaps “What’s the ratio of X to Y according to the report?”), a static RAG would have to either do it approximately in text or ignore it. An agent could retrieve the relevant numbers, then call a calculator tool to compute the ratio, and finally report the result. This multi-tool capability broadens the scope of tasks your AI system can handle autonomously. Essentially, agentic RAG can evolve into an AI assistant that not only fetches information but can act on it or transform it as needed.

    • Robustness via Adaptation: Perhaps the biggest win is robustness. If the initial approach does not work, the agent can try alternatives - different data sources, re-framing the question, etc. In traditional RAG, developers often have to anticipate failure modes and either hard-code fallbacks or accept that the system will occasionally say “I don’t know”. With an agent, some (not all, very important to note this) of that burden is shifted to the agent itself, it can detect “I didn’t find anything useful” and autonomously attempt an informed retry. This doesn’t guarantee success every time, but it often improves success rates in finding an answer.


    All these enhancements need to be balanced with careful oversight and consideration. In critical applications (e.g., medical or legal), you might still prefer a more deterministic retrieval pipeline with human verification. But for many enterprise and general applications, agentic RAG offers a powerful way to build more intelligent, autonomous assistants that leverage both knowledge and reasoning.
